newsitem.title: USA: Loss of jet deal may force McDonnell restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Loss of jet deal may force McDonnell restructuring.

text.p: The Pentagon's decision to eliminate McDonnell Douglas Corp. from the race to build a next-generation fighter jet may force the defence giant to consider a drastic restructuring, analysts said.

"This will be something of a wakeup call," CS First Boston analyst Peter Aseritis said. "It's a fairly sharp and dramatic blow to McDonnell Douglas and I would venture to guess one they probably didn't see coming."

On Saturday the Pentagon awarded four-year contracts to Boeing Co., and Lockheed Martin Corp. to develop prototype fighter jets that could meet the early 21st century requirements of the U.S. Air Force, Navy, Marine Corps and British Royal Navy.
The contracts are worth a total of $2.2 billion including engines, but the ultimate winner would gain control of a military bonanza worth as much as $500 billion.

"Certainly in terms of the overall future, 10 years and beyond, it is a significant programme to us," a disappointed Harry Stonecipher, McDonnell Douglas chief executive officer, told reporters. "This was clearly a surprise to us."
British and U.S. forces have announced plans to buy 3,000 of the joint strike fighter jets, with initial delivery scheduled for 2008.

With potential export sales of another 2,000 jets and additional funding for development, operations and support, the programme could be worth $200 billion to $500 billion over the coming decades, industry executives said.

While McDonnell Douglas is the number two defence contractor and a long-time leader in fighter jets, the St. Louis-based company has failed to win a major role in any of the next generation of tactical aircraft.

Already the smallest of the three major commercial jet makers, the company said last month it would not continue to compete against Boeing and Europe's Airbus Industrie in the market for the biggest jets.

Industry analysts said McDonnell Douglas remained strong with existing fighter contracts and other projects including the C-17 cargo jet but now may be more likely to look for an acquisition or merger.
"Clearly this would raise the prospect of further consolidation," said Nick Heymann of Natwest Securities.

For Boeing, the victory was a major step in the company's continuing march to diversify beyond its highly cyclical core business of commercial aircraft. "I don't want this to be a single-product company," Boeing chief executive officer Phil Condit said. "I want it to be a diversified aerospace company that is good in a number of areas."

Analysts said the military's choice of Boeing -- which has not built a fighter jet since the Army's P-26 "Peashooter" in the 1930s -- underscored the Pentagon's commitment to emphasise cost rather than performance at any price.

Even if Boeing failed to win the "flyoff" and final award in 2001, the company's experience in cutting costs in the highly competitive commercial aircraft market would become increasingly valuable on military platforms, Heymann said.
For number one defence contractor Lockheed Martin, the victory capped a week that included two other major Pentagon awards.

Still, analysts said Boeing would be the team to beat in the competition if its engineers could deliver on their promise to cut costs by building the three versions of the fighter jet with more than 90 percent of their parts in common.
"They very badly want to win," Lockheed aeronautics President Micky Blackwell told reporters. "We're going to have our hands full."
